questions.pre: For the past forty years, software only asked you one question:
Now, software is beginning to answer a different question:

definition: Agentware is the software paradigm built for the agentic era. Instead of operating interfaces step by step, you issue a delegation to software—defining the goal, setting the boundaries, and specifying the acceptance criteria. Within its authorized scope, the system understands context, autonomously organizes actions, adapts to changes, and delivers verifiable outcomes.
shiftTitle: In the past, humans operated software. Now, humans delegate to software.
shiftIntro: For decades, software was built around Features. Software provided buttons and forms, while humans acted as the sole dispatch center—you had to know which app to open, which button to click, which form to fill out, and in what order. Software offered fragmented capabilities; humans were responsible for stringing those capabilities together into outcomes.
Agents have transformed this relationship and rewritten the division-of-labor contract between humans and machines:

eras.body: Paths are hard-coded in advance. Humans click step by step; software passively responds.
AI accelerates single-point tasks (writing, drawing, coding), but humans still have to stitch every step together.
Humans entrust goals and constraints; software understands the task, plans autonomously, executes actions, observes feedback, and adapts dynamically until the outcome is delivered.

shiftClosing: This shift is not about bolting AI onto every piece of software—it is about rewriting software itself.
notTitle: Adding AI does not make it Agentware.
notLead: The difference lies not in whether a large language model is called, nor in whether there is a chat window, but in how the software operates beneath the surface.

notItems.name: AI Feature
notItems.body: Summarization, translation, search, and autocomplete are merely AI features inside traditional software. Efficiency improves, but the work is still operated and completed by humans.

notItems.name: Chatbot Wrapper
notItems.body: Adding a chat sidebar to legacy software, or wrapping a thin shell around a model API, still leaves old software underneath waiting for humans to click step by step.

notItems.name: Rigid Workflow
notItems.body: Fixed A → B → C → D pipelines are traditional automation. A workflow that freezes the moment reality deviates from presets lacks the ability to adapt to context and feedback.

notItems.name: Ungoverned Agent
notItems.body: Wild agents that loop blindly inside a black box with runaway costs and unverifiable outputs are experimental toys—not production-ready software.

archBody: Agentware does not replace deterministic code; it takes over the highest-level control logic. Beneath the surface remain rigorous databases, APIs, and business rules; at the top, "pre-written operation paths" give way to "organizing actions around goals at runtime."
tableRows: Generated dynamically at runtime (Intent → Plan → Act → Adapt → Verify)
Stateless across sessions; resets every time
Explicit governance, auditable, interruptible at any time
loopTitle: Paths are generated at runtime; outcomes are verified before delivery.
loopFlow: Deliver (or Escalate to Humans When Out of Bounds)
loopPrinciple: Goals can be delegated, and paths can be adaptive; permissions must be explicit, outcomes must be verifiable, and processes must be governable.
pillarsLead: For software to truly accept delegations, it must be built upon four foundational pillars:

pillars.lead: The fundamental unit of software shifts from features to delegations.
pillars.body: Traditional software starts by asking "what feature to build"; Agentware starts by asking "what outcome to entrust to the system." A clear delegation defines just four things: what outcome is desired, within what boundaries to act, what qualifies as acceptance, and when to hand control back to a human.

pillars.lead: Not just giving answers, but getting the job done.
pillars.body: Humans are no longer required to script every step in advance. The system determines the next move based on the goal and current state, acts upon the real world through real tools (APIs, MCP, CLI, browsers, databases, software systems), and advances through a closed loop of Plan → Act → Observe → Adapt.

pillars.lead: The greater the autonomy, the more vital the governance.
pillars.body: Agentware is not an unconstrained autonomous agent, but software equipped with execution power inside explicit authorization boundaries. Governance is just as critical as execution—every delegation must make clear: what it is permitted to do, what it actually did, how much cost it incurred, who can halt it at any moment, and how to roll back safely when errors occur.

pillars.lead: Memory transforms software from a one-off tool into a continuously evolving system.
pillars.body: Software without memory starts from zero every time; traditional retrieval (RAG) is merely passive document lookup. Agentware's memory system does more than answer questions—it directly participates in planning, decision-making, and action:
points: Preserves both the full context of specific tasks (episodic memory) and abstracted cognitive rules (semantic memory).
Breaks knowledge down into minimal intelligible units, automatically deduplicating, merging, revising, and distilling as new information arrives.
Every distilled memory can be traced back to its original source—auditable and trustworthy.

manifestoIntro: Software used to be a tool waiting to be operated. It provided functions; humans had to learn it, orchestrate it, and take responsibility for the results. Now, for the first time, software can be delegated work. This is not about bolting AI onto legacy software—it is about redefining what software should be in the age of agents.

manifesto.en: Software should understand intent, not just input.
manifesto.body: In the past, humans had to translate their goals into a sequence of clicks and forms. Now, humans state what they want and what they won't accept—and software is responsible for understanding.

manifesto.en: Software should execute goals, not just expose functions.
manifesto.body: No matter how many features exist, humans still had to string them together into outcomes. The value of software lies not in how many functions it exposes, but in what outcomes it delivers.

manifesto.en: Paths may adapt. Outcomes must remain verifiable.
manifesto.body: Reality rarely unfolds according to preset workflows; execution paths must adapt to environment and feedback. The freer the path, the clearer the goal and acceptance criteria must be.
We do not pursue unbounded autonomy. Every delegation must have explicit accountability and an auditable trail, always preserving human authority to intervene, roll back, and take over.

manifesto.en: Memory turns software from a tool into an evolving system.
manifesto.body: A one-off executor starts from scratch every single time. Software that remembers context, accumulates experience, and refines itself grows to understand its people and organization better with every use.

manifesto.en: The future unit of software is not the feature. It is the delegation.
manifesto.body: In the past, designing software meant asking, "What feature goes here?" Today, designing software means asking, "What outcome should be entrusted to it?" Define the goal, boundaries, and acceptance criteria—and let the system complete the rest.

studioTitleEn: Exploring the paradigm. Sharing the knowledge. Building the tools.
studioTitle: Exploring the paradigm. Sharing the knowledge. Building the tools.
studioIntro: Agentware Studio is an independent research and creation studio dedicated to the Agentware paradigm. At the inflection point where software shifts from "operating interfaces" to "delegating intent," we advance the adoption and evolution of this paradigm through deep research, open curriculum, and product experiments:

studioItems.title: Paradigm Research & Essays
studioItems.body: We continuously document and publish in-depth essays and field notes on software design in the agentic era, memory architectures, human-agent collaboration contracts, and the future of work—offering a clear intellectual framework for understanding next-generation software.

studioItems.title: Open AI Engineering Curriculum
studioItems.body: Moving from "operating software" to "delegating to software" starts with upgrading human mental models and methodology. We are producing a structured AI engineering curriculum—from foundational mechanics to hands-on system building—to help everyone master core capabilities for the agentic era:
seasons: Stripping away the hype—from next-token prediction, tokens, hallucinations, and context windows to RAG, tool calling, and Agents—understanding when to trust AI and how to put it to work.
When code becomes cheap and judgment becomes scarce, learn how to write specs for AI, design architecture before touching code, and distill personal expertise into reusable Skills.

Grounded in real-world scenarios—covering context engineering, workflow orchestration (n8n / Dify), MCP server development, multi-agent collaboration, safety guardrails, and evaluation pipelines to turn real workflows into autonomous systems.

studioItems.title: User-Facing AI Tool Experiments
studioItems.body: Ideas must ultimately be validated by products. At aikit.pro, we continuously design and ship user-facing AI tools and applications, exploring how "software that acts on intent" feels in everyday workflows.
